extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of natural philosophy / scholars of the philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for conducting and judging natural-philosophical (scientific) inquiry as articulated in Bacon's Novum Organum and the editor's commentary. Emphasises method, the relation of experiment and reason, institutional impediments, and intellectual virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake formal method for true knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid being impressed by elaborate methodical partitions and forms which appear to 'comprehend and conclude everything' about a subject while in fact their parts are poorly filled and empty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware authors who present sciences in a polished, personated form that seem 'perfect' though the constituent parts are weak; prefer substantive results over ostentatious schemes. Anti-pattern: valuing completeness of taxonomy or partitioning as if it were empirical or explanatory success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distrust impostors and extravagant promises
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sceptical of those who, by credulity or imposture, burden humanity with grand promises (life-prolongation, transmutations, divination, occult revelations, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate vain novelties and charlatanry from genuine arts; use past impostures as a caution against accepting new extravagant claims without rigorous proof. Example anti-patterns: alchemical/magical promises accepted on mere assertion or spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not convert technical failure into claims of natural impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors often turn the infirmity of their art into a calumny upon nature, declaring that what their art cannot achieve is impossible in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid asserting that limitations of current arts or techniques reflect limits of nature itself. Encourage attempts to extend art rather than pronouncing phenomena impossible. Anti-pattern: treating inability to effect in practice as proof of impossibility in principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek diverse instances; do not confine attention to the same cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Phenomena that appear secret or occult in some instances may be manifest and common in others; experiments and contemplations confined to the same instances will never reveal the full nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary experimental contexts and examples; examine different materials and conditions since the same nature may present differently. Anti-pattern: repeatedly observing only one kind of instance and concluding universal secrecy or absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep natural philosophy methodologically independent of theological authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural philosophy must be arrived at by a purely independent process, employing only scientific data and submitting only to scientific tests; theological prepossessions must not hamper investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science should be judged and defended on scientific grounds; theologians may co-ordinate scientific results with doctrine but must not preclude investigation. Anti-pattern: using scriptural or ecclesiastical authority to suppress or discredit empirical findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defend intellectual freedom within educational institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities, colleges, and schools often arrange lectures and exercises so that new thoughts do not easily occur; dissenters are chastised as turbulent and lovers of novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage liberty of judgment and toleration of dissent in academic settings; avoid curricula and disciplinary practices that imprison students within authoritative authors. Anti-pattern: curricula that force rote adherence to established authors and penalise inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide proper incentives and social recognition for scientific advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Great increases in science come from great minds, yet rewards and prizes for sciences typically lie with the populace or princes who are rarely well learned; progress is often deprived of both patronage and popular praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise and suitably reward substantial scientific contributions to encourage further advances; be aware that lack of reward deters major efforts. Example: innovators without patronage are less likely to succeed or be sustained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turn past errors into arguments for future progress (grounds of hope)
rubrics_metrics.description: The very errors and false ways pursued in past times are the best grounds for hope in the future: each impediment known from former errors gives an argument for correction and improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catalogue and analyse historical errors to identify remedies and to justify optimism for further progress. Example: Columbus's rejected reasons were later experimentally validated; use such exemplars to motivate investigation rather than despair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate empirical (experimental) and rational (theoretical) faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who have studied sciences have been either empirics (mere accumulators) or dogmatics (weavers of theories); the ideal is a middle role (the bee) that extracts matter from experience and transforms it by reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extremes of mere collection without understanding (formica) and pure speculative systems (aranea); seek a rigorous union of experiment and rational analysis. Anti-patterns: purely empirical piles of facts without interpretation; purely deductive systems detached from experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mathematics appropriately: inductive establishment before quantitative deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics should terminate (formalise and quantify) the axioms of natural philosophy only after those axioms have been carefully established by induction; mathematics then enables deductive quantitative work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First establish general axioms inductively from experiments; then state them in quantitative form and combine deductively using mathematics. Anti-pattern: letting mathematics or pure deduction generate physics without prior inductive grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purge common notions and prejudices from the mind before inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Human reason is a mixture of faith, chance, and early-formed puerile notions and farrago; no one has yet had the constancy to abolish common theories and notions entirely and apply the intellect fresh to particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work to cleanse the understanding of inherited commonplaces and first impressions so as to let particulars be observed and judged without distorted preconceptions. Anti-pattern: unquestioned reliance on received common notions when examining particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose plausible conjectures and exemplars to stimulate enterprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjectures and illustrative demonstrations (e.g., Columbus's reasons for lands to the west) should be set forth to open hope and induce industry in experiment and inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish and exhibit well-reasoned conjectures and worked examples to awaken confidence and enterprise among investigators; use such exemplars as a part of preparing minds. Anti-pattern: withholding plausible hypotheses for fear of error, thereby discouraging exploration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance hope with prudence; call upon civil prudence when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: While hope is essential to drive inquiry, prudent civil judgment should be consulted because some expectant projects may involve risks and social consequences; lighter hopes should be set aside in favour of those with more firmness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate visionary aims from those with stronger grounds; consult sober judgment and counsel to avoid imprudent pursuits. Anti-pattern: unbridled optimism without weighing practical dangers or societal impacts.
